title: Bridge Networking Among Namespaces
markdown:
# Bridge Networking Among Namespaces

A single `veth` pair connects exactly two interfaces — one host end, one namespace end. That works fine for one namespace, but the moment you need *three* namespaces to all talk to each other, pairwise veth links stop scaling: three namespaces need three direct pairs, four need six, and every new namespace means wiring a new link to every existing one. Real multi-container hosts never do this. Instead, every container's veth pair connects to a shared **Linux bridge** — a single virtual switch inside the kernel — and the bridge forwards traffic between however many members are attached to it. This is exactly the mechanism behind Docker's default `docker0` bridge: every container gets one veth pair to `docker0`, and `docker0` handles the rest.

In this lab you will build that mechanism from scratch: one bridge, three namespaces, three veth pairs — and you will prove that two namespaces which have **never** been directly wired to each other can still reach one another, purely because they share a bridge.

## Why Not Just Keep Adding veth Pairs?

With direct veth pairs, connecting `ns1` to both `ns2` and `ns3` means creating two separate veth pairs just for `ns1` — one per peer. Add a fourth namespace and now you need three more pairs just to keep everyone mutually connected. The complexity grows as the square of the namespace count, and every namespace ends up juggling a different interface name for every peer it talks to.

A bridge flips this: each namespace gets exactly **one** veth pair, connecting it to the bridge — not to any other namespace directly. The bridge, acting as an L2 switch inside the kernel, looks at the destination MAC address of every frame it receives on one port and forwards it out whichever port that address lives on (or floods it to all ports if it doesn't know yet, the same way a physical Ethernet switch does). From each namespace's point of view, it looks exactly like being plugged into a shared switch alongside every other namespace — because that is precisely what is happening.

| What | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `br0` | The Linux bridge — the shared virtual switch every namespace connects to |
| `veth-hostN` / `veth-nsN` | The Nth veth pair — `veth-hostN` stays on the host and joins the bridge, `veth-nsN` moves into `nsN` |
| `10.70.0.11/24`, `.12/24`, `.13/24` | Addresses for ns1, ns2, ns3 — all on the **same** subnet, because they all sit behind the same bridge |

## Part 1: Building the Bridge

A bridge is itself a network interface — you create it the same way you create any other virtual device, with `ip link add ... type <kind>`, just with `kind` set to `bridge` instead of `veth`.

```bash
sudo ip link add br0 type bridge
sudo ip link set br0 up
```

Unlike a veth pair, a bridge does not come with a built-in peer — it starts out as an empty switch with zero ports. You attach interfaces to it one at a time with `ip link set <iface> master <bridge>`, the same `master` keyword used for any device being enslaved to a bridge, bonding device, or team interface.

> **Note:** A bridge interface must itself be `up` to forward traffic between its members — bringing up each individual veth end is not enough on its own.

## Part 2: Wiring ns1, ns2, and ns3 to the Bridge

Each namespace follows the identical four-step pattern:

1. Create the namespace
2. Create a veth pair
3. Move one end into the namespace, keep the other on the host
4. Attach the host-side end to `br0` with `master`, bring everything up, assign the namespace-side address

### ns1

```bash
sudo ip netns add ns1
sudo ip link add veth-host1 type veth peer name veth-ns1
sudo ip link set veth-ns1 netns ns1

# Join the bridge
sudo ip link set veth-host1 master br0
sudo ip link set veth-host1 up

# Bring up the namespace side and address it
sudo ip netns exec ns1 ip link set lo up
sudo ip netns exec ns1 ip link set veth-ns1 up
sudo ip netns exec ns1 ip addr add 10.70.0.11/24 dev veth-ns1
```

`ip link set veth-host1 master br0` is the step that matters most here — it is the only thing that distinguishes this lab from a plain veth-pair setup. Everything else (bringing interfaces up, assigning an address) is identical to what you have done in earlier labs.

### ns2 and ns3

Repeat the exact same pattern, incrementing the number each time:

```bash
# ns2
sudo ip netns add ns2
sudo ip link add veth-host2 type veth peer name veth-ns2
sudo ip link set veth-ns2 netns ns2
sudo ip link set veth-host2 master br0
sudo ip link set veth-host2 up
sudo ip netns exec ns2 ip link set lo up
sudo ip netns exec ns2 ip link set veth-ns2 up
sudo ip netns exec ns2 ip addr add 10.70.0.12/24 dev veth-ns2

# ns3
sudo ip netns add ns3
sudo ip link add veth-host3 type veth peer name veth-ns3
sudo ip link set veth-ns3 netns ns3
sudo ip link set veth-host3 master br0
sudo ip link set veth-host3 up
sudo ip netns exec ns3 ip link set lo up
sudo ip netns exec ns3 ip link set veth-ns3 up
sudo ip netns exec ns3 ip addr add 10.70.0.13/24 dev veth-ns3
```

Notice that all three namespaces land on the same `10.70.0.0/24` subnet. That is deliberate — a bridge operates at Layer 2, so every member needs an address in the same Layer-3 subnet for routing to make sense, exactly like every device plugged into a physical switch normally shares one LAN segment.

### Checking Bridge Membership

```bash
ip link show veth-host1
```

You should see `master br0` appended to the interface's flags line — this is how you confirm an interface has actually joined a bridge, as opposed to merely existing on the host unattached.

**Why it matters**: this is precisely what `docker network inspect bridge` is showing you when it lists a container's `veth` interface as a bridge member — the exact same `master` relationship, just created and torn down automatically by the Docker daemon instead of by hand.

## Part 3: Proving the Bridge Actually Bridges

Here is the payoff. `ns1` and `ns2` have never been directly wired together — neither has `ns1` and `ns3`. The only thing connecting any of them is that each has its own private veth pair into `br0`.

```bash
# ns1 -> ns2
sudo ip netns exec ns1 ping -c 3 10.70.0.12

# ns1 -> ns3 — the real test: these two share no direct link whatsoever
sudo ip netns exec ns1 ping -c 3 10.70.0.13

# and the reverse direction
sudo ip netns exec ns3 ping -c 3 10.70.0.11
```

All three succeed. `ns1`'s packets to `10.70.0.13` go out `veth-ns1`, arrive at `veth-host1`, get forwarded by `br0` to `veth-host3` (the port where that address lives), and arrive at `veth-ns3` inside `ns3` — three hops through the bridge, with `ns1` never needing to know anything about `ns3` except its IP address.

**Why it matters**: this is the full-mesh connectivity every container on a Docker bridge network gets for free. You never manually wire container A to container B — you attach both to the same bridge, and the bridge handles forwarding between any pair of members, including pairs added long after the bridge was first created.

## Conclusion

A Linux bridge solves the scaling problem that direct veth pairs create: instead of O(n²) point-to-point links between namespaces, every namespace needs exactly one veth pair into a shared bridge, and the bridge forwards between all of them.

- `ip link add <name> type bridge` creates an empty virtual switch
- `ip link set <iface> master <bridge>` attaches an existing interface to it as a member port
- Every bridge member needs an address in the same subnet, since bridging happens at Layer 2
- Two namespaces with no direct link can still reach each other purely through shared bridge membership

This is not an abstraction unique to this lab — it is the literal mechanism `dockerd` uses to create `docker0` and attach every container's veth pair to it. Understanding `ip link ... type bridge` and `master` is understanding how `docker network inspect bridge` and `brctl show` (or its modern `ip link show type bridge` equivalent) actually work underneath.
